War Without a Vote

A week of unauthorized war-making, voter-suppression pressure, and courts pushing back on executive overreach

```markdown This was a week defined by a war the president started on his own authority and then struggled to explain, alongside an escalating campaign to rewrite the rules of American voting, and a judiciary that kept intervening to check both. By week's end, gas prices had spiked to levels unseen in years, a synagogue and a university ROTC program had both been attacked, and courts in three separate cases had told the executive branch it had exceeded its lawful authority.

The weekend began with the launch itself. Trump initiated air and naval operations against Iran alongside Israel without seeking congressional war authorization, a break from precedent that Republican leaders defended as falling within the president's inherent powers. The rhetoric escalated almost immediately: a Miami summit floated using military force against Latin American drug cartels and even raised the possibility of regime change in Cuba, suggesting the administration saw the Iran operation as a template rather than an isolated action. That same weekend, a federal court intervened on a separate front: Judge Royce Lamberth ruled that Kari Lake's appointment as acting head of the U.S. Agency for Global Media had violated the Vacancies Act, voiding her mass layoffs of more than 1,000 Voice of America journalists and her reduction of the agency's broadcast languages from 49 to four. Lake said she would appeal, but the ruling stood as an early marker of judicial pushback against unconfirmed executive appointments — a pattern that would recur before the week was out.

Violence touched the weekend directly as well. Two teenagers who described themselves as ISIS supporters threw improvised explosive devices during dueling protests outside New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's residence. Neither device detonated, and both suspects were charged with federal terrorism offenses, but the incident underscored how the atmosphere of the moment was drawing extremist actors near the seats of elected officials. Separately, a three-year prosecution of a Cop City protester concluded with an Alford plea: John Mazurek avoided conviction but accepted a decade of probation barring him from anti-government protest activity, closing out a case that had involved extended pretrial detention and surveillance later found to raise Fourth Amendment concerns. And the EPA repealed the scientific finding underpinning federal greenhouse gas regulation, even as the Justice Department simultaneously argued in court that federal law preempted state climate superfund laws — a contradiction state attorneys general said undercut the government's own legal position.

By Monday, the administration's demand for a new voting law had become explicit. Trump began pressing Congress to pass the Save America Act — legislation requiring proof of citizenship, banning most mail voting, and folding in unrelated culture-war provisions — and said he would not sign other legislation until it passed. The same day, the Supreme Court struck down Trump's tariff regime as exceeding presidential authority, opening the door to potentially $175 billion in corporate refunds and triggering an immediate wave of lawsuits. Monday also brought a significant oversight story: reporting revealed that DHS's civil rights and detention ombudsman offices had been cut by more than 90 percent, even as at least 15 people died in ICE custody during fiscal year 2025 — the highest total in years — and congressional investigators documented 510 credible abuse allegations, some involving children. Separately, the White House ordered a hold placed on an FBI, DHS, and National Counterterrorism Center bulletin warning of elevated domestic threats tied to the Iran war, blocking it from reaching state and local law enforcement. A federal grand jury also subpoenaed Arizona's state legislature for records from its 2020 election review, which Trump celebrated publicly and Arizona's attorney general called an effort to weaponize federal law enforcement against a settled election. The administration additionally ended Temporary Protected Status for roughly 2,500 Somali nationals despite a documented hunger crisis and active terrorism risk in Somalia. And on the war itself, Trump's messaging began to fracture: he told one outlet the war was "very complete" while telling House Republicans "we have won in many ways, but not enough" — a contradiction that would deepen as the week went on.

Tuesday sharpened both storylines. Senators emerged from a classified Iran briefing frustrated by unanswered questions about war costs, the possibility of ground troops, and the absence of any coherent postwar plan; Senator Warren invoked Congress's power of the purse as a potential check. That same day, officials were caught in a string of false statements — Trump wrongly claimed Iran possessed Tomahawk missiles and denied U.S. responsibility for a strike on a girls' school, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright falsely claimed the Navy had escorted a tanker through the Strait of Hormuz before deleting the post. The Pentagon also revised its public estimate of wounded troops sharply upward, from fewer than a dozen to as many as 150, only after independent reporting forced the correction. Judicial pushback continued as well: Judge Matthew Brann ruled that three New Jersey federal prosecutors installed by Attorney General Bondi to bypass Senate confirmation had been illegally appointed, echoing an earlier ruling in the Alina Habba case and reinforcing the pattern of courts rejecting unconfirmed executive appointments. In Utah, Republicans moved to block withdrawal of signatures from an anti-gerrymandering repeal petition and expanded the state supreme court from five to seven justices, a maneuver critics described as court-packing meant to blunt adverse redistricting rulings. Meanwhile, the human and financial costs of the war became visible to ordinary Americans: gasoline in California topped $5 a gallon and oil prices hit their highest levels since 2022 as the Hormuz shipping crisis deepened, contradicting earlier administration claims that the situation was nearly resolved.

Wednesday brought the most direct challenge yet to the war's stated justification. U.S. intelligence agencies told congressional staff privately that available intelligence did not support Trump's claim that Iran had been preparing an imminent strike — the rationale originally given for launching the operation. The top Democrat on the intelligence committee said he had seen no evidence of such a threat. The same day, Trump said he did not know about a military investigation finding the United States responsible for a strike that killed at least 175 people, mostly children, at an Iranian girls' school, and separately claimed the U.S. had struck 28 mine-laying ships despite earlier reporting of only sixteen. Civil society responded in kind: a broad coalition including the ACLU, AFL-CIO, and Planned Parenthood Action Fund announced a national day of action for March 28, with more than 3,000 planned events aimed at surpassing an earlier mobilization of roughly seven million participants. Separately, organizers reported a surge in federal tax resistance, with training-session attendance jumping from a dozen to nearly 500 people in a single month. House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile, declined to condemn explicitly Islamophobic remarks made by two Republican members of Congress, and the administration's Medicare and Medicaid overseer announced plans to remove millions more people from ACA coverage rolls.

Thursday was the week's most consequential day for the voting-rights storyline. The House passed the Save America Act, with its citizenship documentation requirements, voter ID mandates, mail-ballot restrictions, and criminal liability provisions for election officials, while Trump publicly pressured Senate Majority Leader Thune to gut the filibuster to force the bill through — a request Thune refused. The same day, Senator Tim Sheehy physically joined Capitol Police in ejecting an Iran-war protester, a Marine veteran, from a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing, an altercation that left the protester with a broken arm; Sheehy blamed the protester for "causing violence." Thursday's gravest event came in Michigan, where a naturalized U.S. citizen drove a vehicle into Temple Israel synagogue in West Bloomfield Township and was killed during the incident. The FBI later described the attack as retaliation for Israeli strikes that had killed the attacker's relatives in Lebanon; 140 children in the synagogue's preschool were unharmed. The Pentagon also disclosed that war costs had already surpassed $11.3 billion in six days, a figure covering munitions alone, while the White House dismissed as "fake news" reporting that it had badly underestimated Iran's willingness to close the Strait of Hormuz.

The week closed with a cluster of judicial rulings that, taken together, formed one of its clearest patterns. Judge James Boasberg quashed a grand jury subpoena targeting Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, finding "abundant evidence" that it was intended to pressure Powell over interest-rate policy rather than to investigate any actual wrongdoing. A federal judge in Oregon separately found that ICE had conducted warrantless arrests without probable cause, driven by a national quota of 3,000 daily arrests, and halted the practice while criticizing the agency's targeting methods. And FCC Chairman Brendan Carr threatened broadcasters with the loss of their licenses over coverage of the Iran war that the administration deemed "fake news," drawing bipartisan criticism, including from a Republican senator. Violence recurred as well: a gunman with a prior ISIS material-support conviction opened fire during ROTC training at Old Dominion University, killing one person and injuring two before being subdued and killed by students. On the international front, the administration eased sanctions on Russian oil shipments to calm markets rattled by the war, a move Germany's chancellor said allies had explicitly urged against. And new economic data showed the underlying strain: fourth-quarter GDP growth of just 0.7 percent alongside rising core inflation, as munitions depletion and mounting war costs pressed against the wider economy.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a single throughline across seemingly separate stories: a president exercising war powers without a vote, pressing for voting restrictions without full legislative consent, and encountering, again and again, a judiciary willing to say that specific exercises of executive power had crossed a legal line. Courts voided an unlawful media takeover, invalidated unconfirmed prosecutors, blocked a retaliatory subpoena against the central bank, and struck down warrantless immigration arrests — four distinct rulings against four distinct abuses of appointment and enforcement power, arriving within the same seven days. Meanwhile, the human costs mounted outside the courtroom: rising fuel prices, contradictory casualty figures, a synagogue attacked, a university classroom attacked, and immigration detention oversight hollowed out even as deaths in custody reached a multi-year high. None of these threads resolved by Friday. But together they showed a system under real pressure — from the executive branch pushing at the edges of its authority, and from courts, protesters, and ordinary institutional friction pushing back. ```
